There's a famous legal case about this very thing called Terasoff v. California. What happened was that Ms. Terasoff was having sexual relations with a pajit. She broke off the relationship, which broke pajit's mind. He was apparently lucid enough to seek psychological treatment, wherein he confided in the psychologist a concrete, well-planned desire to kill Ms. Terasoff. The doctor did nothing. Pajit carried out his plan. Ms. Terasoff's parents then sued, saying the doctor had a duty to inform the police when pajit told him about his plan. The court agreed, and set some ground rules that are now called the Terasoff Doctrine.

Essentially, if you are in treatment, and you tell your therapist that you:

  • Desire to harm yourself or others;
  • Have a concrete plan for how you're going to do it;
  • Have the means of carrying it out; and
  • Plan to carry out the plan imminently,

the therapist is required to break confidentiality and inform the authorities.
